ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, the closed rectangular conducting coil abcd rotates at a uniform speed in a uniform magnetic field around the symmetry axis OO′ perpendicular to the magnetic induction lines. Observed along the OO′ direction, the coil rotates clockwise. It is known that the magnetic induction intensity of the uniform magnetic field is B, the number of turns of the coil is n, the side length of side ab is L1, the side length of side ad is L2, the coil resistance is R, and the angular velocity of rotation is ω. When the coil rotates to the position shown in the figure, what is the direction of the induced current in the coil?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the rectangular conducting coil is located in the plane of the paper, and the uniform magnetic field is represented by multiple horizontal arrows pointing to the right, with B marked beside it; the dashed line OO′ is the vertical symmetry axis passing through the center of the rectangle; the four vertices of the rectangle are labeled as upper right a, upper left b, lower left c, and lower right d; near O there is a rotation arrow of angular velocity ω, and the stem states that, observed along the OO′ direction, the coil rotates clockwise. Then reason: At the time shown in the figure, the magnetic induction lines are in the plane of the rectangular coil, so the magnetic flux passing through the coil is at the zero-flux position. Judging according to the clockwise rotation direction given in the problem, the coil is just rotating past this zero-flux position; if the positive direction of area matched with the loop a→b→c→d→a is taken, then the magnetic flux of the external magnetic field passing through the coil is increasing in the negative direction, that is, the positive magnetic flux is decreasing. According to Lenz's law, the magnetic field produced by the induced current should hinder this change in magnetic flux, so it should produce magnetic flux consistent with the positive direction corresponding to a→b→c→d→a. Using the right-hand screw rule to judge, the circulating direction of the current that can produce a magnetic field in that direction is a→b→c→d→a.
